title.en: The Wise Matanga, Outcast Ascetic (Matanga Jataka, no. 497)
title.zh: 摩登伽賤種聖者本生（第四百九十七）

texts.period: Jataka no. 497, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Benares and the kingdom of Mejjha, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈與彌闍國（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A Candala-born ascetic is beaten for defiling a rich girl's eyes, wins her as his wife, and stages a false descent from the moon as Great Brahma; her proud son Mandavya later reviles the same sage at an alms-hall, is twisted by city goblins, healed by the sage's rice-leavings, and outcasted with the other brahmins - while the kingdom whose king kills the sage is annihilated by hot ashes.
summary.zh: 賤種出身的聖者摩登伽因「不祥」被商人女眷僕從毆打，後娶得此女，假扮大梵天自月輪降世；其子曼達耶於施捨場辱罵聖者，被城中鬼神扭頸，賴聖者剩飯得癒，卻與眾婆羅門同被逐出種姓——而後殺害聖者的彌闍國被天神降下熱灰燼滅國。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this tale of king Udena, who had once broken a basket of red ants over a meditating elder. Long before, in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a Candala's son named Matanga. When the merchant's daughter Dittha-mangalika caught sight of him at the city gate she cried that she had seen an ill omen, washed her eyes with scented water, and her crowd beat the innocent man senseless. Matanga resolved never to move until he had her, and lay at her father's door for seven days until the girl was given to him. He kept her honourably, then left for the forest and in seven days mastered the eight attainments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Matanga Jataka (no. 497) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: He returned as the Great Brahma: Dittha-mangalika was coached to say her husband had gone to Brahma's heaven and would return at the full moon breaking the moon's disk. On that night the sage blazed through the sky, thrice circled Benares, descended, and touched her navel, leaving her with child and a prophecy that kings would pay tribute at her feet. Her son Mandavya grew rich, feeding sixteen thousand brahmins daily. When the ragged sage stood at the gate, Mandavya reviled him as a vile outcast and bade his servants kill him; the sage rose into the air - reviling a sage, he warned, avails as much as swallowing blazing fire - and the city deities, avenging him, twisted Mandavya's neck backwards and left the brahmins writhing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Matanga Jataka (no. 497) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: His mother fetched the sage's rice-leavings as an elixir: Mandavya rose cured and ashamed, and the sixteen thousand brahmins, having tasted a Candala's leavings, were put out of caste and moved to the king of Mejjha. Matanga next humbled the proud ascetic Jatimanta: his dropped tooth-sticks floated upstream into Jatimanta's hair, and when the ascetic cursed him to die with a bursting head, Matanga held the sun from rising until Jatimanta was dragged to him with a lump of clay on his head and plunged into the river. Later, men of Mejjha killed the sage for his alms-food; the deities rained hot ashes and wiped that kingdom from the earth. Udena was Mandavya, the Master said, and I was the wise Matanga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Matanga Jataka (no. 497) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: King Sivi Gives His Eyes (Sivi Jataka, no. 499)
title.zh: 屍毘王施眼本生（第四百九十九）

texts.period: Jataka no. 499, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Aritthapura, kingdom of Sivi, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 屍毘國阿利提城（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Sivi, unsatisfied with six hundred thousand pieces a day in alms, vows to give part of his very self; Sakka tests him as a blind brahmin asking for an eye, the surgeon removes one and then the other, and by an Act of Truth on the worth of every suitor Sivi's eyes regrow as eyes of Truth that see a hundred leagues.
summary.zh: 屍毘王日施六十萬錢猶感不足，誓以身體所有施人；帝釋化作盲婆羅門索眼，御醫先後剜其二目，王無悔意；因誓願諦實，雙目重生為「諦實之眼」，能透山越牆遠觀百由旬。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: King Sivi of Aritthapura kept the ten royal virtues and gave six hundred thousand pieces daily at six alms-halls. Sitting on his throne on a full-moon day he decided that outside things no longer satisfied him: if a suitor asked his heart he would cut it out as one lifts a water-lily from a lake; if his flesh, he would carve it off; if his blood, he would fill a bowl with it; and if any demanded his eyes, he would pluck them out as one draws the pith from a palm-trunk. Bathed and adorned, he rode to the alms-hall to meet whatever came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sivi Jataka (no. 499) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sakka, king of the gods, resolved to test the vow and took the shape of an old blind brahmin on a mound, stretching out his hand. The courtiers wept and offered pearls, coral, chariots and elephants instead; the king answered that a man who swears to give and then withholds puts his own neck in a snare. The surgeon Sivaka protested, then loosed the right eye with burning powders, severing the hanging ball; blood stained the royal robes. Gazing with his remaining eye, the king set the eyeball in the brahmin's socket, where it fixed like a blue lotus in bloom - and then, thrilled by the joy of the gift, he gave the second eye also.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sivi Jataka (no. 499) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Blind, Sivi handed his kingdom to his courtiers and withdrew to the park as an ascetic; Sakka's marble throne grew hot, and he came down to offer any boon. The king asked only death - for he was blind. Sakka bade him make an Act of Truth upon his gift. Whoever comes to ask of me, the king declared, he is dear to my heart: and one eye grew in the empty socket, then the other - eyes neither natural nor divine, but eyes of Truth Absolute that see a hundred leagues through rock and wall. Restored, the king preached to all Sivi: never eat food without giving something away. Ananda was the surgeon, Anuruddha was Sakka, and I was King Sivi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sivi Jataka (no. 499) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Rohanta the Golden Deer King (Rohanta-miga Jataka, no. 501)
title.zh: 金鹿王本生（第五百零一）

texts.period: Jataka no. 501, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山羅訶塔湖（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Rohanta, golden king of eighty thousand deer, supports his blind parents in the Himalaya; snared at the drinking-place, he stays mute until his herd is safe, and his brother and sister refuse to abandon him though he begs them to flee; the softened hunter frees him, and with golden hairs as token teaches the Law in the queen's name to satisfy her dream-craving.
summary.zh: 金鹿王羅訶塔率八萬鹿群居喜馬拉雅，奉養失明雙親；於飲水處被獵人羅網所縛，先忍不發聲以免群鹿驚散，弟妹寧死不離；獵人動憫放生，鹿王贈金毛，教其代為說法以滿王后夢中求聽金鹿說法之願。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: When Brahmadatta ruled in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a golden stag in the Himalaya named Rohanta, king of eighty thousand deer, with a golden brother Citta-miga and golden sister Sutana; all three served their aged blind parents beside Lake Rohanta. A dying hunter told his son of the golden deer, and when Queen Khema dreamed of a gold-coloured stag preaching the Law with a voice like a golden bell, she woke crying for it. Feigning a woman's craving, she threatened to die without hearing such a stag, and the king sent the hunter's son with money to snare him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Rohanta-miga Jataka (no. 501) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The snare was set at the drinking-place. Caught at the pole's end, the Great Being stood feigning to drink until all eighty thousand had drunk and withdrawn; only then did he jerk at the noose - once till the skin split, twice till the flesh, thrice till the tendon - and raise the cry of capture. His brother Citta refused three times to flee: I am ready to lay down my life, I will not leave thee here. The doe Sutana ran a little way in fear, then returned to die beside him. The hunter came up with his spear, guessed they were born of one womb, and heard Citta plead: slay him and you slay all five, for he supports his blind parents; grant him life and you bestow life on us all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Rohanta-miga Jataka (no. 501) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hunter cut the thong, washed the blood away, and by his love and the Bodhisatta's perfection the wound closed without a mark. Learning the queen's craving was the cause, the stag bade him stroke his back - the hand came away covered with golden hairs - and taught him ten stanzas on the holy life to preach in his stead. The hunter recited them on a golden throne; the queen's craving was satisfied, the king heaped rewards on him, and the man chose instead to become an ascetic in the Himalaya. Channa was the huntsman and Sariputta the king; I was myself the royal stag Rohanta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Rohanta-miga Jataka (no. 501) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince of the Iron House (Ayoghara Jataka, no. 510)
title.zh: 鐵室太子本生（第五百一十）

texts.period: Jataka no. 510, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A jealous co-wife's prayer turns her into an ogress who devours two newborn princes; the third is born and raised for sixteen years in an iron house; paraded for his coronation, the prince counts womb and prison as two hells, refuses the kingdom in a torrent of stanzas on death, and walks out - with his father, court and the whole city following him to the hermitage Sakka has built.
summary.zh: 妒妻咒願成羅剎，連吞二位新生王子；第三子於鐵室中降生並被囚養十六年；及至登基出巡，太子自省：十月處母胎如糞獄，十六年居鐵室如牢獄，縱脫羅剎之手仍不免老死——遂連篇偈頌堅辭王位出走，父王、臣民舉城相隨，入帝釋所造精舍出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: A barren co-wife of the Benares royal house prayed in anger to devour her rival's offspring, and was reborn a goblin. When the queen bore her first son the goblin snatched him before her eyes and crunched him like an onion; a second child met the same fate. When the Bodhisatta was conceived the king summoned all the smiths of the realm and built a house wholly of iron, pillars and all, lit continually with lamps; there the queen bore a marked prince, named Ayoghara-kumara, the Prince of the Iron House, while the ogress perished seeking the water of Vessavana to drink.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ayoghara Jataka (no. 510) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: At sixteen the king resolved to set the kingdom on him, and the prince, decked for coronation, made his circuit of the decorated city and asked the courtiers what fault was his that he had been caged so long. None, they said; a goblin devoured your brothers, and the iron house saved your life. He pondered: ten months in my mother's womb were as the Hell of Dung, sixteen years in this prison as the Ussada hell; and though I have escaped the goblin I have not escaped old age and death. In twenty-four stanzas he declined the throne - no warlike prowess stays death, no juggler's trick cozens it, no serpent's venom or physician's skill - and asked his father's leave for the religious life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ayoghara Jataka (no. 510) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king refused. Then, as a mad elephant bursts his steel chains and a young lion breaks out of a golden cage, the prince burst his carnal desires, saluted his parents, and departed; his father cried that he wanted no kingdom and went with him, and the queen, the courtiers and every soul in Benares left their houses behind and followed - a crowd twelve leagues long - into the hermitage Sakka had caused to be built. The king's parents were that royal pair, and I was myself the Wise Ayoghara.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ayoghara Jataka (no. 510) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The King's Debt to the Man-Ogre (Jayaddisa Jataka, no. 513)
title.zh: 勝武王償羅剎債本生（第五百一十三）

texts.period: Jataka no. 513, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Kingdom of Kampilla, Northern Panchala, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北般闍羅劍浮沙國（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A queen's rival became an ogress and devoured two princes but reared the third on human flesh; generations later that man-eater waylays King Jayaddisa, who buys a day's grace to pay a brahmin, and the crown prince Alinasattu goes in his father's place, wins the ogre's reverence by his fearlessness, proves him the king's long-lost uncle, and converts him to the ascetic life.
summary.zh: 王后情敵墮為羅剎，吞食二位王子，卻將第三子當獸撫養、以人肉為食；多年後此人形羅剎攔路擒獲勝武王，王以須償婆羅門偈金為由乞一日之期；太子勝軍代父赴約，無畏供身，感化羅剎，並查明其實為王之失散長兄，勸其出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: A queen's rival in the harem prayed to devour her offspring and became an ogress. Twice she seized and crunched the newborn prince; the third time guards turned her away before she could eat, and the child, suckling at her breast out of ignorance, kindled a mother's love: she hid him in a rock-cave of the cemetery and fed him on human flesh until, losing the magic root that masked his shape, he prowled the forest road as a man-eater. The fourth prince, born safe after her death, was called Jayaddisa, the Victor, and his son was Alinasattu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Jayaddisa Jataka (no. 513) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Jayaddisa, who had promised a brahmin four stanzas worth a hundred pieces each, was returning from the hunt with a slain antelope when the ogre leapt up crying: after seven days' fast, a mighty prey at last. The king offered him the venison and was refused; he offered nothing but truth - a promise made to a brahmin is still unpaid - and the ogre gave him till dawn. He paid Nanda the brahmin four thousand pieces, told his son, and set out to die; but Alinasattu would not have it: if you go I will follow you, and both alike will cease to be - and the king let the boy go in his place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Jayaddisa Jataka (no. 513) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: To the ogre the prince offered his own body freely: eat me and free my father, for death I do not fear - I have weighed birth and death in this world and the worlds to be. Sent to gather firewood for his own pyre, he returned with a blazing pile and bade the ogre stand no longer gaping but take and slay him; the ogre confessed that to eat one so truthful would burst his skull in seven pieces. The prince, noting that the creature's eyes were red and unwinking yet cast a shadow, declared him no ogre at all but his father's lost brother, proved it before a clairvoyant ascetic, and left him ordained in the forest while the king founded the town of Cullakammasadamma for the ascetics' support. The man-eater was Angulimala, and prince Alinasattu was myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Jayaddisa Jataka (no. 513) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kingdom Where Everyone Cursed the King (Gandatindu Jataka, no. 520)
title.zh: 萬民詛咒昏君本生（第五百二十）

texts.period: Jataka no. 520, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Kingdom of Kampilla, Northern Panchala, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北般闍羅劍浮沙國（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A tree deity - the Bodhisatta - admonishes the careless king Pancala in eleven verses, then guides the disguised king and chaplain through villages where a thorn-pierced elder, an old mother with unwed daughters, a ruined ploughman, a kicked milkman, children mourning a calf skinned for a scabbard, and even a frog eaten by crows all curse the king by name; chastened, the king rules righteously ever after.
summary.zh: 菩提薩埵化身丁多迦樹神，以十一偈諫誡怠政的般闍羅王；王與國師喬裝出巡，沿途聽聞老者足刺荊棘、老嫗之女無人可嫁、犁伕失牛、賣乳者被牛踢翻、童子哭祭被剝皮製鞘的小牛、乃至乾塘中青蛙被烏鴉啄食——無不指名咒罵國王；王乃懺悔，自此行正法治國，廣行布施。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: King Pancala ruled unrighteously in the kingdom of Kampilla: oppressed by taxation, his subjects took wives and children to the forest like wild beasts, fencing their empty houses with thorn branches and hiding all day. The Bodhisatta was then the divinity of a tinduka tree outside the city, honored yearly with an offering worth a thousand pieces; pitying his benefactor, he stood in mid-air at the king's bedhead one night, bright as the new-risen sun, and admonished him in eleven verses: zeal is the way to Nirvana, sloth leads to death; a slack king is no master of his realm, and the careless sink here to ruin and hereafter to hell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gandatindu Jataka (no. 520) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Chastened, the king handed his kingdom to his ministers and went out with the chaplain disguised. In the first village an old man's foot was pierced by a thorn as he barred his house at dusk, and he cursed the king by name; the chaplain tried to excuse him, but the elder answered that by night they are prey to thieves and by day to the king's men, and lewd folk abound when evil kings bear sway. In the next village an old mother fallen from a bush cursed Brahmadatta because her two grown daughters lived unwed; a ploughman whose ox fell under the ploughshare cursed him; a milkman kicked by a vicious cow cursed him; children who saw a calf skinned for a sword-sheath while its mother roared and pined cursed him; and when the pair reached a dry tank where crows were striking frogs, the Bodhisatta put the curse into the frog's mouth too - and when the chaplain defended the king, the frog answered that the king, though people are oppressed, deems the priest's policy the best.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gandatindu Jataka (no. 520) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king and his priest concluded that every creature down to the frogs in the forest cursed them, returned to the city, and ruled thenceforth righteously, devoting themselves to charity and other good works. The discourse was really preached to the king of Kosala; the divinity of the tinduka tree was myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gandatindu Jataka (no. 520) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The Miser Who Would Not Share a Drop (Sudhabhojana Jataka, no. 535)
title.zh: 慳吝財主本生（第五百三十五）

texts.period: Jataka no. 535, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Benares and the riverbank forest, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈與河畔林間（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Six generations of Treasurers gave away eighty crores and rose from god to god; the sixth, Maccharikosiya, burns down the family alms-halls, hoards everything, and steals into the forest to cook a secret porridge rather than feed a single guest - until Sakka and his four heaven-born descendants descend as beggars, spoil his meal with a shape-changing dog, and preach him back to generosity.
summary.zh: 連續六代財主皆散盡八億家財布施，依次生於帝釋、月天、日天等天界；第六代慳吝者拆毀施捨堂、分文不施，為獨享一口甜粥竟瞞著妻子僕人潛入林中自炊——帝釋攜四代子孫化身婆羅門相繼登門乞食勸化，以化形之犬穢其食、化形之馬驚其魂，終令其散盡家財、出家修道。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: In Benares a householder of eighty crores begged the king's leave to give it all away, built six alms-halls, spent six hundred thousand daily, and was reborn as Sakka; his son, grandson, and great-grandsons kept the tradition and rose in turn to be Canda, Suriya, Matali and Pancasikha. But the sixth, Maccharikosiya, judged his ancestors fools: I will guard my treasure and not give a penny to a soul. He burned the alms-hall, drove beggars from his gate, and lived himself on rice and sour gruel in coarse garments under a leaf parasol, rolling his money together and neither enjoying it nor sharing it with wife or children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sudhabhojana Jataka (no. 535) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeing the sub-treasurer eat sweet porridge, he conceived a craving he dared not utter lest anyone demand a share: night and day he thought of nothing but porridge and grew pale, hugging his bed. His wife guessed it; he bargained her down from a city-wide feast to a single pot, took the rice, milk, sugar and honey himself, and went alone to cook it in the forest by the river, posting a slave as lookout. On his yellow-marble throne Sakka saw the family tradition destroyed, gathered his four descendants, and came down as brahmins, one after another, each preaching over the miser's protest: from little give little, from much give much; eat not alone - no bliss is his that by himself shall dine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sudhabhojana Jataka (no. 535) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Groaning, Maccharikosiya seated all five brahmins and served the porridge; then Pancasikha became a dog that fouled the cooking-pot, and when the miser threatened it, a blood-horse of shifting colours; the brahmins rose and stood fixed in mid-air. Who are ye? he cried, and Sakka answered: Canda and Suriya, Matali the charioteer, Pancasikha chasing thee - and I, Sakka. Misers and scorners of brahmins are reborn in hell; the steadfast in right, who give alms, abide in heaven. We came not for the porridge, said Sakka, but out of pity for thee. Then Kosiya poured out his whole treasure for the beggars, built a hut of leaves between the Ganges and a natural lake, and took the ascetic life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sudhabhojana Jataka (no. 535) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.
